etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English spire, spyre, spier, spir, from Old English spīr, from Proto-Germanic *spīrō, *spīrǭ (“peak; point; tip; stalk”). Cognate with Dutch spier, German Low German Spier, German Spier, Spiere, Danish spir, Norwegian spir and spire, Swedish spira, Icelandic spíra.

definitions.definition: (now rare) The stalk or stem of a plant. [from 10th c.]
A young shoot of a plant; a spear. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1913, D[avid] H[erbert] Lawrence, “Chapter 12”, in Sons and Lovers, London: Duckworth & Co. […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Clara had pulled a button from a hollyhock spire, and was breaking it to get the seeds.

definitions.definition: Any of various tall grasses, rushes, or sedges, such as the marram, the reed canary-grass, etc.
A sharp or tapering point. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1907 January, Harold Bindloss, chapter 1, in The Dust of Conflict, 1st Canadian edition, Toronto, Ont.: McLeod & Allen, →OCLC:
quote.text: A beech wood with silver firs in it rolled down the face of the hill, and the maze of leafless twigs and dusky spires cut sharp against the soft blueness of the evening sky.

definitions.definition: (architecture) A tapering structure built on a roof or tower, especially as one of the central architectural features of a church or cathedral roof. [from 16th c.]
The top, or uppermost point, of anything; the summit. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ix]:
quote.text: the spire and top of praises

definitions.definition: (mining) A tube or fuse for communicating fire to the charge in blasting.
(of a seed, plant etc.) to sprout, to send forth the early shoots of growth; to germinate. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto V”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: In gentle Ladies breste and bounteous race / Of woman kind it fayrest Flowre doth spyre, / And beareth fruit of honour and all chast desyre.

quote.citation: 1707, J[ohn] Mortimer, The Whole Art of Husbandry; or, The Way of Managing and Improving of Land. […], London:  […]  J[ohn] H[umphreys] for H[enry] Mortlock […], and J[onathan] Robinson […], →OCLC:
quote.text: It is not so apt to spire up as the other sorts, being more inclined to branch into arms.

definitions.definition: To grow upwards rather than develop horizontally. [from 14th c.]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old French spirer, and its source, Latin spīrō (“to breathe”).

definitions.definition: One of the sinuous foldings of a serpent or other reptile; a coil. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1700, [John] Dryden, “Alexander’s Feast; or, The Power of Musique. An Ode, in Honour of St. Cecelia’s Day.”, in Fables Ancient and Modern; […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: A dragon's fiery form bely'd the god: Sublime on radiant spires he rode.

definitions.definition: (geometry) The part of a spiral generated in one revolution of the straight line about the pole.
